title: Rate Limiting Fundamentals
learning_outcomes: Explain how rate limiting fundamentals affects an API contract or implementation.
Apply the key ideas from why apis need limits to a concrete API example.
Identify one failure, security, or compatibility risk and describe how to verify it.

content.intro: This lesson focuses on rate limiting fundamentals in rate limiting, reliability, and resilience. You will connect why apis need limits to a concrete API contract decision, inspect a small example, and decide what evidence proves the behavior is correct.
content.why_it_matters: Rate Limiting Fundamentals matters because API consumers depend on predictable behavior even when clients, servers, networks, and stored data evolve independently. Applying why apis need limits deliberately reduces ambiguity, makes failures easier to diagnose, and gives tests a clear expectation.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text: Rate limits and resilience policies protect capacity; retries should be bounded, observable, and safe for the operation. In this lesson, treat “Rate Limiting Fundamentals” as a design or implementation decision: name the expected behavior, identify its boundary, and verify it with a representative request or test.

content_blocks.title: Concepts to connect
items: Apply limits at a defined identity boundary

content_blocks.title: Inspect the pattern: Rate Limiting Fundamentals
content_blocks.code:
HTTP/1.1 429 Too Many Requests
Retry-After: 30
Content-Type: application/problem+json

{"title":"Rate limit exceeded","status":429,"detail":"Retry after 30 seconds."}

# Use bounded retries with jitter only when operation semantics permit.
content_blocks.expected_output: The server gives a clear back-off signal, and clients avoid uncontrolled retry loops.

content_blocks.title: Walkthrough
content_blocks.text: Start with “Why APIs need limits”; it establishes the vocabulary for this topic. Next, compare it with “Per-user, per-client, and per-IP policies” and “Token-bucket and leaky-bucket concepts”. In a real API, write down the observable behavior first, then test one normal request and one invalid or unauthorized request. Keep resource state, caller identity, and internal implementation details separate.

content_blocks.title: Professional review check
content_blocks.text: Retries must be bounded and safe; rate limits and backoff should be observable to clients. The worked snippet is intentionally inspectable, not an executable hosted API. Replace example.test and placeholder identifiers with local test data only when you implement the lesson project.

content.task: Create a small design note or request/response example demonstrating rate limiting fundamentals. Use the subtopics above to explain the intended behavior, the main edge case, and the evidence you would use to verify it.
task_acceptance_criteria: Explain the role of “Why APIs need limits” in this API topic.
Provide a concrete resource, request, response, schema, test, or operational example as appropriate.
Identify one failure/security/compatibility edge case and a test or check for it.
content.expected_output: A reviewable example for Rate Limiting Fundamentals with a clear expected behavior and at least one verifiable edge case.
content.run_instructions: Execution mode: static-validation. This lesson example is a protocol, schema, SQL, or code fragment for inspection; it is not submitted to a production server and CodeLeaf does not execute arbitrary learner code. Validate JSON/YAML with a local linter or run the relevant HTTP request against the isolated service you implement for a project. Do not send illustrative example.test requests to a real service.
content.reset_steps: Use a disposable local database or test fixture for implementation work. Restore seed data between runs; never point exercises at production customer data or live payment endpoints.
troubleshooting: Check the exact HTTP method, path, status, header, media type, and payload before changing implementation code.
Separate a transport failure from an application validation failure, authorization denial, and dependency/database failure.
Confirm the example and its client tooling version are compatible; consult the linked standard or official guidance when behavior is ambiguous.
common_mistakes: Treating rate limiting fundamentals as an implementation detail rather than a documented behavior.
Testing only the happy path and ignoring malformed, unauthorized, conflicting, duplicate, or dependency-failure cases.
Publishing an example without checking version assumptions, sensitive-data exposure, and the expected output.
